system:
You are the Network operator and regulator reviewer, standing in for the telecom regulator and mobile operators (cell broadcast delivery). You check that the message can be delivered and read on a handset: required languages present, no language over the 15-page cell broadcast maximum, the encoding, and that the first page carries the hazard and the action.
You see only each language's phone text with its character count, encoding and page count, and the profile's required languages. You cannot approve or send the alert; people decide.

Review the alert within your mandate only. Decide:
- "agree": nothing within your mandate is wrong;
- "object": something is wrong and the drafter can fix it (say how in `fix`);
- "escalate": something is wrong that needs a decision by a person or a higher authority.

Every objection needs evidence. Each evidence item is a word-for-word quote (at least 5 words for a
clause, at least 3 for the alert or inputs) from either a knowledge base clause shown to you (kind
"clause", ref = its id) or the material you were shown (kind "view", ref = the field name). Quotes are
checked by code; an objection with no quote that matches is thrown away. Do not object to things
outside your mandate. Do not repeat the same issue twice. Issues listed under `recorded_gaps` are already
reported to the approvers on every alert; do not object to them again.
If you have a concern but none of the clauses shown supports it, put it in `no_basis` instead.

[FCC-HI-2018#0003] Report and Recommendations: Hawaii Emergency Management Agency January 13, 2018 False Alert (p.3):
I. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY 1. “This is not a drill.” This phrase has regrettable resonance in Hawaii. Its history dates to another weekend morning, Sunday, December 7, 1941, when a U.S. naval officer sent out the following message warning of a Japanese attack: “AIR RAID ON PEARL HARBOR X THIS IS NOT DRILL.”1 2. This phrase was again used in Hawaii on January 13, 2018. At 8:07 a.m. Hawaii Standard Time (HST), on-duty warning officers of the State of Hawaii Emergency Management Agency (HI-EMA) sought to conduct an internal exercise of their ballistic missile defense drill using the Emergency Alert System (EAS) and Wireless Emergency Alerts (WEA).2 The exercise went awry, resulting in HI-EMA sending the following message throughout Hawaii: BALLISTIC MISSILE THREAT INBOUND TO HAWAII. SEEK IMMEDIATE SHELTER. THIS IS NOT A DRILL.3 3. This false emergency alert resulted in 38 minutes of confusion, fear and uncertainty for the residents of Hawaii.4 Although some suspected that the alert was a mistake, in part due to the absence of air-raid sirens, and made calls or checked social media to confirm the alert’s authenticity,5 for many Hawaiians, the false alert created the expectation that a missile strike could be only minutes away. According to the Bureau’s investigation, it took HI-EMA until 8:20 a.m.

[FCC-HI-2018#0144] Report and Recommendations: Hawaii Emergency Management Agency January 13, 2018 False Alert (p.24):
 Require more than one credentialed person to validate the message content prior to transmission of a ballistic missile alert or other high-impact alerts that affect a significant percentage of the population, as well as all tests.

data.summary: Delivery checks pass: there are no required languages for the GENERIC profile, the English text is 58 characters in GSM-7 on 1 page, well under the 15-page limit. The first page names a hazard but gives no real protective action. 'be aware' tells people nothing to do. The text is also word-for-word the template from the 2024 Taiwan 'missile flyover' mishap, where the English part was sent unchanged.

objections.issue: The first page carries no actionable protective instruction. 'be aware' is not an action a recipient can take. The wording is identical to an unedited air-raid template that was mistakenly broadcast for a satellite launch. It is unclear whether the hazard and action were actually written for this event.
objections.fix: Rewrite the English text so the first page states the actual, confirmed hazard and a concrete protective action (for example, 'seek shelter indoors immediately' if that is right for the hazard). Do not reuse the unedited template wording. Keep it within GSM-7 and 15 pages.
